utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And for your reference, Colonel Konings, your expert report is at the second tab. Now, if we could move to section 10 (B) of the expert report, which appears on page 11 in the English version and page 26 in the B/C/S version. Now, you will see, Colonel Konings, in section 10 (b) you state: "One has always to remember that artillery and mortars are by their nature aerial weapon systems." Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber what you mean by an aerial-weapon system.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Yes. What I try to explain there is that the word "area" stands against the word "point," and an area is -- is a larger area, for example, 100 by 50 metres or 200 by 200 metres, opposite a single point which can be a single vehicle. And up until, let's say, the mid-1990s artillery was developed and was used as an area coverage system because of the fact that the ballistic -- the ballistic features of an artillery or mortar is such that no round will fall on the same spot as a -- as you have aimed at that. That is done by various factors like propellant temperature, outside temperature, the characteristics of the specific gun, we call it gun-to-gun variations. So there are main variations externally that have an influence on the ballistic trajectory of a projectile, which makes them -- makes them fall apart to each other. For that reason when you combine the fire -- a fire mission of several guns or several Howitzers, you get a natural spread out of the points where the actual projectiles are falling and exploding which we call an area coverage opposite a point coverage.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. A bit further in that same section you state: "The common used munitions do not have precision capabilities and are therefore not very suited to engage point targets." You have already touched a bit on what you consider to be a point target. Can you then explain why artillery is not well, suited to attacking, for example, a vehicle or a small house?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, as I explained, the round-to-round variation, even if you fire from the same gun or the same Howitzer is in such a way that it is very hard to hit with one gun a small target, because of those variations that differ from round to round, rounds will not fall on the same spot. There is an story that soldiers that are attacked by artillery use an artillery crater to hide themselves because in that same crater, no following round will fall. That is, of course, a theoretical approach but, in fact, it is true. There are very few artillery guns, Howitzers or mortars that are so precise that you can you use them in combatting a point target. And when you want to use an artillery gun to combat a point target, you need a substantial number of rounds to be able to hit it in such a way that it will be either destroyed or neutralized.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And let's move on to section 6 (b) (iii) which appears on page 6 of the English version and page 13 of the B/C/S. Now in section 6 (b) (iii) Colonel Konings, you state: "Artillery is not the weapon system to destroy strong buildings, armoured command vehicles and the like." And I'd like you to explain to the Chamber why artillery is not the weapon system to destroy strong buildings?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, that has to do with the nature of the technical build-up of an artillery or mortar projectile which is -- you need explosive power to destroy things, and an artillery projectile has just not enough explosive strengths to destroy a strong concrete or brick building. It may damage it, it may take pieces of it, but for destruction, and the word destruction means take it out completely, take it out of it's original function, that's, in most cases when you have a strong building, just not possible. As I have seen many times in Sarajevo where you have some superficial damage on the outside, and, of course, you will destroy windows, and, of course, you will have damage, but the destruction is some other thing, especially when you have a multi-storey strong building, it is it not possible to destroy that building completely with artillery or mortar projectiles unless you are willing to spend several hundreds of projectiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you then tell the Chamber what kinds of targets artillery is good for attacking and why?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Artillery in itself is with -- let's put it the old-fashioned ammunition which is the high-explosive round and what was in use up until now, is very good in combatting unarmoured, unprotected targets like infantry personnel in the open, or personnel in the open - it doesn't need to be infantry - unarmoured vehicle columns, logistic supply areas, lightly armoured vehicles, lightly armoured command post. That kind of targets are ideal, especially when they are somewhat larger, they are ideal to -- to use artillery or mortars against them.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's now please move to section 11 of your expert report, where you discuss the destructive power of artillery projectiles, and this appears at page 12 of the English version and page 28 of the B/C/S. Now, I'm looking specifically at section 11 (c) where you describe the most common type of projectile which you have just mentioned as the high-explosive. And first I'd like you to tell the Chamber whether or not high-explosive projectiles were in use in 1995?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, high-explosive projectiles were very common projectiles and in use in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And in subsection C-2 you indicate that a fragmentation projectile can produce several thousand fragments and that they can range up to hundreds of metres. First, I'd like to you clarify for the Chamber whether fragmentation, as you call it, is the same thing as shrapnel, and if not, what's the difference.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Basically there is -- no, not basically. There is no difference. Fragmentation is the process of the breaking apart of the steel case of a projectile, and that delivers those thousands of shrapnels or fragments that fly around and do their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you also clarify whether this range of hundreds of metres for the fragmentation is based on the projectile striking the ground or exploding in the air.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Basically that -- that is a -- is a common position, but once you choose for exploding the projectile in the air, the fragments -- there are more fragments available because when the projectile detonates on the soil or against a building, part of the projectile disappears in the soil. It is not effective anymore. But once you use an explosion above the ground, practically all the fragments will fly through the air, will fly further and will do more damage than when you use a point-detonating or a detonation on the ground. But both explosions, both types of explosions, will produce those thousands of fragments.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you clarify the distinction between the range of hundreds of metres that you mention here and the "absolute lethal distance of 50 metres"?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: I have used that as an example for a 155-millimetre Howitzer projectile that is in the infantry of our own army. And the absolute lethal distance means that when you are within a 50 metre radius of the point of explosion, the concentration of the density of shrapnels in the air is so high that it will kill everyday inside that radius. That is what I mean by absolute lethal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And subsection (c) (iii), you include some additional cyphers. And I would ask you to please explain those to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, again that is taken to give you an example how far those projectiles can come, and they are -- they, of course, do not stop when they cross the border of the 1600 square metre that I figure here, but it gives you an idea that you can cover with one projectile an area of 1600 square metre by fragments, and those fragments at the edge of those area may not be absolutely lethal but will cause damage and will cause injuries, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. At subsection (c) (vi) (2) -- I'm sorry, (c) (vi), you describe some factors that could enlarge the effect of artillery projectiles. And in subsection 1, you describe one such factor as the explosion being inside of a house. First, I'd like you to describe for the Chamber how you get a projectile to explode inside of a house, as opposed to on the outside of it, and then I'd like you to explain to the Chamber what would be visible from the outside if the projectile exploded inside?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, depending on the strength of the wall or a house or a building or a vehicle, a projectile can penetrate. If the wall is too strong, the projectile will either explode on the outside or will just bounce off against the wall, and even you have the chance that it will not explode. But once the projectile -- the wall is soft enough to -- to allow penetration or in case you use a concrete-piercing fuse, that means that the fuse is strong enough to make the projectile going into the building, then have you an explosion inside a room, inside a concealed area, and then the pressure function, the blast function of the projectile is making its work besides, of course, the fragmentation, but the pressure cannot escape to a free area, the pressure builds up very quickly. Because that's what happens with an explosion. You have a very high peak pressure. And when that pressure cannot escape, for example, into the open air, it will kill a lot of people. It will just throw people against walls. It will depress lungs, et cetera, et cetera. It will give a very nasty incidents. And I witnessed that myself in Sarajevo various times that a projectile entered a house, and at the outside of the house you only see a hole, a large hole with no further visible damage at the outside of the house, but inside the complete house can be collapsed. The first floor came down and came down on the ground floor and killed all the people inside either by the rubble that came down or by the pressure that came down, or fragments, but the effect that you wanted to achieve, is achieved.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, at subsection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. ... yes, yes. Mr. Konings, it is only until now that the French translation has caught up. Could you try to make a break now and then or to talk a bit more slowly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Turning to subsection (c) (vi) (2), Colonel Konings, you indicate that the use of an variable time fuse to detonate a projectile between 6 and 20 metres above the ground gives the maximum effect against uncovered personnel and unarmoured vehicles. And I would like to you please explain to the Chamber what exactly a variable time fuse is.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: A variable time fuse is a -- well, is in it itself a fuse that contains a small radar system which starts working once you fire the projectile and makes -- and takes care of the fact that the projectile explodes at the desired height above ground. So it is a simple construction, a small radar system inside the nose of the projectile that receives the return beam from the radar on six metres high and then triggers the projectile to explode which brings the projectile to explode at 6 metres high. And for the same function, one can use a normal time fuse that is nothing more, nothing less than a clock system, a kind of watch that is inside the fuse, which counts the seconds after the shot is fired and, for example, 35 seconds after the projectile has left the barrel, the projectile explodes. And if you have done your calculations right, it is about 10 metres or 6 metres or 20 metres above the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And can a normal time fuse, as you call it, be used with any kind of artillery shell?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: A normal time fuse has only one limitation -- or all fuses have their limitation that they basically only can use with a certain calibre. So if you have a 122-millilmetre Howitzer, they have their own types of fuses, and a 155-millimetre has only its own type of fuses. But every known type of Howitzer or gun in every army inventory, they do have point-detonating fuses and probably also variable time fuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber whether the normal time fuses which you have described were available and in use in 1995?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Time fuses, normal time fuses were available and wide spread in use in, I think, nearly every army in the world in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you tell the Chamber whether the explosion of a time fuse set projectile is commonly referred to, or what is commonly referred to as an air-burst?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Well, you could -- you could use that term for a -- a projectile that is used in combination with a time fuse or a variable time fuse. That causes an air-burst, an explosion of the projectile on a certain height in the air. So air-burst is a correct word for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's please move now to section 11 (d) of your expert report, and this appears in the English version on page 13. In the B/C/S, on page 29. And in that section, Colonel Konings, you describe a special category of high-explosive projectiles which you referred to as DPICM for dual purpose improved conventional munition. And I would like to you please describe for the Chamber what that is.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: A DPICM munition is a -- what we call in military terms a carrier projectile which is a thin projectile-shaped case, and in there you find a number of submunitions sometimes also referred to as cluster munitions. And depending on the length of the projectile and the calibre, you will find a certain number of submunitions in there. The 155 projectile that the Netherlands army has had in its inventory was containing 88 submunitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber whether or not these kinds of cluster munitions were in use in 1995?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Just some clarification. In use by the HV or used throughout the world?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the previous answer, the witness himself, because the same came to my mind, gave the answer where he said that almost all the armies --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, but if we first ask the witness to respond to the question, and he is now certainly aware that by use by whom is, of course, relevant to know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Your Honour. I cannot tell you -- I do have the knowledge if DPICM ammunition was in use with the HV army, with the Croatian army, I do not have that knowledge. I do know that the Bosnian Serb army used that type of ammunition because I witnessed that myself inside Sarajevo. But I do not have the knowledge about the Croatian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Since we're on that topic, Colonel Konings, do you know whether or not the United States or Germany had these type of cluster munitions?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I object to the relevance of whether or not the United States or Germany had cluster bombs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the relevance can be linked up later, but the issue of where the HV were being supplied from could also indicate where or what might be at their disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me. Outside the presence of the witness, I'd like a good faith proffer from Mr. Russo as to why he is asking that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, is there any way that you reserve that question for a later stage or is it -- because then we could deal with it at ten minutes to 7.00, but in the absence of the witness, it seems not to be a subject to be discussed in his presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm happy to do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we delay our discussion on the matter, and then we'll hear from you at a later stage. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Now, Colonel Konings, you mentioned that the Netherlands Army used or had cluster munitions for a 155-millimetre. Was that a Howitzer weapon?

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: That was a Howitzer weapon, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And can you tell the Chamber whether these cluster munitions can be used with any kind of artillery weapon, whether it be a Howitzer, a gun, a rocket system, or a mortar?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the relevance of this -- there is no relevance to it. The witness doesn't even know if the HV had cluster munitions available to it. It is completely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Konings, could I -- I'm not going to ask you whether you speak English because you do, but therefore, unfortunately, I have to ask you perhaps to leave this courtroom for a second because the parties are having a dispute on a matter which is preferably discussed in your absence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could remain stand by.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe, one of the last sentences spoken by you was that the witness doesn't even know if the HV had cluster munition ammunition available to it. From what I feel, and let me just -- I get the impression that Mr. Russo seeks to establish that it was -- whether they had it or not, certainly that it would have been within their reach perhaps. Now, that is not per se irrelevant even if you do not know perhaps by other evidence which you could establish that they, even if this witness doesn't know, that they got hold of it, I do not know. I have got no idea, but that seems to be the issue. And that, of course -- the Chamber will finally evaluate the evidence in its totality. Now, if there's anything specific, Mr. Russo, that -- because you could, or course, go through all the armies of the world and then establish their diplomatic relations with that countries, and therefore, it would not that might not reach the level of relevance which would be appropriate to use. Is there anything specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, the -- first, Mr. President, you're correct in regard to the aim of my questioning being to establish the general availability of these kinds of munitions in that time-period. And also if the Court will recall during the testimony of Witness Dawes who testified to having observed cluster munitions in Knin, the Chamber specifically requested the parties to provide the Chamber with information about what kinds of weapon systems could deliver cluster munitions. Clarify that thens who testified to having observe the cluster munitions. That was the purpose of asking Mr. Konings the question of what kinds of weapon systems could deliver those munitions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: The reality is that there is no evidence in possession of the Office of the Prosecutor of, one, that the HV had cluster bombs in the area of the former Yugoslavia. The normal system that carried cluster bombs was an Orkan rocket such as fired by the ARSK on Zagreb. Two, there has been no evidence presented by the Office of the Prosecutor that this has been -- the United States or Germany or any other country supplied Orkan rockets or cluster bomb system to the HV. It is certainly not in this witness's report, and it's certainly not in any of the evidence that the OTP has turned over. Now, if there some basis upon which the Office of the Prosecutor in good faith can argue that the HV fired cluster bombs in an Orkan rocket type system or in some type of 155 system, they have not produced it. And I asked production of that as a basis -- good faith basis for these questions. It is wild speculation to ask about any weapon system that is potentially on the market in 1995. Certainly if the HV had the opportunity to do that, they wouldn't have been firing the 155s that they from the JNA that they were using, that were in many cases, years and years old. This is wild speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, on wild?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I stand by wild speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm asking a question to Mr. Russo in which I expressed that I had carefully listened to your observations, Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe it is any kind of speculation wild or otherwise. I have already pointed the Chamber to the evidence which has come in to the trial already through Witness Dawes that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give us an -- I take it that you checked that. Could you give us a reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I haven't actually checked for the transcript or exhibit, but I can certainly provide that to the Chamber a bit later. In any indication case, I'm sure the Court will find once we provided that Witness Dawes did in both his 92 bis submission and again in court indicate that he saw actually saw cluster bomblets in Knin. That, of course, is direct evidence that cluster munitions were fired into the town. Now, we don't require direct evidence that the HV, in fact, fired those in order to make it relevant as to who could have fired them and what kinds of weapons systems could have delivered those munitions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, Judge, and if I can follow up on the testimony of Mr. Dawes. Number one, he is the only witness who testified to that. All of the other military officials that we saw come into this courtroom, no one said anything about cluster bombs. Number two, upon pressed in cross-examination, Dawes couldn't even remember where the cluster bombs were. He said point A during course of his 92 ter statement that was submitted. During the course of his testimony and the map presented through Mr. Russo, he said point B. That's because the Prosecutor had submitted into evidence the Zasteva film on point a that was taken by the ARSK that showed that there were no cluster bombs in the location that Mr. Dawes said they were. So interesting enough and remarkably enough the location changes to a place where there were no photographs. At the end of the day, and we can pull it up from the transcript, if I can paraphrase Mr. Dawes, he doesn't remember where it was. And put that on top of the fact that as Mr. Russo just said he doesn't know if the HV fired it, or as we know who had it, the ARSK fired it. And Mr. Dawes's testimony began, I believe, on 14 October 2008, page 10501. I am directed to lines 12 to 15. I'm not certain if that is the cross as well as the direct -- that is the cross I'm told. Thank you. Cross is the 14th, and the Chief is, I think, 13th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, the transcript reference for direct can be found on 10482 and 1043. I would just like to respond briefly. First of all, I certainly don't appreciate the implication that somehow Mr. Dawes's testimony was changed as a result of evidence brought in by the Prosecution, but in any case, I don't think it is appropriate for Mr. Kehoe to be testifying about what kinds of weapons systems could deliver cluster munitions. He says it only the Orkan rocket. Mr. Konings is about to testify that, in fact, any artillery system can deliver cluster munitions. I think that's exactly the type of area where the court is assisted by expert evidence as opposed to merely the position taken by the parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I didn't say -- I did not say that other systems couldn't deliver cluster bombs. I did not say that. What I said precisely, and maybe I wasn't clear enough, is that the system that was prevalent in the former Yugoslavia at that time coming out of the JNA was the Orkan rocket system. That was the system commonly used to deliver cluster bombs. Could other systems conceivably have been used, did the JNA conceivably use other systems? That is possible. The bottom line is there not one iota of evidence that has been delivered by the Prosecutor that, one, the HV had cluster bombs that they fired, two, that the United States provided anything like that, or, three, that Germany did. So if it doesn't have any bearing on what evidence we have presented to us, then we are just taking a journey through weapon systems throughout -- not even the western world, throughout the world itself. It is simply irrelevant to the considerations before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, very practically, of course, I'm trying at this moment to -- to read what Witness Dawes and others said about cluster bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I certainly agree with Mr. Kehoe that Mr. Dawes is, in fact, the only witness who provided evidence as to presence of cluster munitions in Knin. I'm certainly not denying that fact. He did indicate that he was unclear as to where exactly he saw them, though he was quite clear that he did, in fact, see them. I don't want do digress into a discussion of circumstantial evidence, but the existence of the cluster munitions in Knin is certainly circumstantial evidence that they were fired into Knin by someone. Now that someone could be, as the Prosecution believes, the HV or, as the Defence would like to suggest, the ARSK. Now, one way or the other, it is relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Kehoe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, isn't the point of this exercise to determine who is at the other end of this gun? If, in fact, whoever is firing that weapon, isn't that the entire artillery case being presented by the Prosecutor? And there are any number of weapon systems we have that have been fired by the HV, T-130s, Howitzers, there were some MRLs fired. There is -- without question, there is not one scratch of evidence to reflect that during the course of this case any evidence is presented that they fired any cluster munitions in all of the documentation presented. None.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Expect for the testimony of Mr. Dawes that cluster munitions were in Knin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, I -- you emphasise that cluster ammunition has been seen; and you emphasise that there is no evidence that the HV used that, so perhaps a matter to resolve. One second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, the Chamber will allow you, within a very strict latitude, some questions to establish a factual foundation. It's not at this moment, but if there's anything this witness could know of which would lay a factual foundation for more than we have in evidence now, that the HV would have had available not just the possibility but whether this witness knows anything about access to -- then you are -- and we'll check after three minutes whether you made any progress.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I'm not sure, Mr. President. The last question I actually had was the last one I asked which was whether artillery weapons -- what kinds could deliver the cluster munitions. And if the witness answered that any kind could which I expect the answer to be, then we are simply going to be arguing to the Court based on the fact that the HV was in possession of certain weapons, any of those could have fired the cluster weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Judge, you know we are in an area of speculation. If we're talking about could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be very -- is there any dispute about that wide variety, wide range of weapons could fire cluster ammunition? If there is no dispute about that, then there is it no need --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Your Honour, I offered that as a proposed stipulation to Mr. Kehoe. He indicated that did he not agree that any type of artillery system could deliver cluster munitions, he said it was only the Orkan rocket system. That's why I'm asking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Certainly in one of his questions referred already to more than the Orkan system. I think he mentioned two systems, but on the other hand, we can spend another ten minutes on the matter. Let's hear from the witness what his answer to this question is. If every type of weaponry could fire it, then we might not know much more, but it certainly goes quicker, and it's not -- in itself, it is not prejudicial to the Defence, I would say. Let's -- The witness is coming in already. So you mentioned the one question you wanted to put the witness. Any other question would be subject to what I just said, Mr. Russo.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: As the witness is coming in, Your Honour, I would ask the Prosecution to note in the report where he is tying this back to the HV because I don't find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Russo, is there any --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I didn't say we were doing that, and I'm not doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Then there is a lack of disclosure on that issue, in any event.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's see what the question is. Mr. Konings, we'll continue. Mr. Russo, your next question to Mr. Konings.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Colonel Konings, before you left, I had asked the question -- and I will simply repeat it here. Can you please tell the Chamber what kinds of artillery weapons systems are capable of delivering cluster munitions.

utterances.speaker: HARRY KONINGS
utterances.text: Capable of delivering cluster ammunitions are the regular types of Howitzers like calibres of 155, 203 millimetres and the comparing calibres like 152 and 122. Besides that, some mortar types are able to deliver cluster ammunition, although that has not been very developed in the past period, and rocket systems are also capable of delivering cluster ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Thank you. I would like to move now to a discussion of some of the general principles that you set forth in your expert report regarding planning of artillery operations, and in particular --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Obviously we have problem with the transcript, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's LiveNote that's frozen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: LiveNote is -- yes, I was still with the transcript of Mr. Dawes, as a matter of fact, so that I didn't notice that. On my -- on one of my screens, I have a perfect transcript and now check on the other. There is a -- it depends on what system I'm looking at, because the --

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: The court system here, Your Honour, appears to be working fine. It is only LiveNote that appears to be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, although the court system is also LiveNote, so I am a bit confused about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: I believe it is the Internet connection that is causing the problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is there -- my last words appear as, "One second, please," which might already be two minutes, please. Is there any way that we can get on our screens that can be manipulated, because the same is true for all of us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the problem is the same everywhere. I suggest that -- we can't use the LiveNote system, which we can manipulate, where we can make our annotations, although scrolling back and access to previous transcripts of other days is also not working. What we have on our screens we can ... I suggest that we keep our eyes on the left screen for the time being, which allows us to look at a little bit over one page. If that causes us problems, I would invite the parties to inform me, because if it gets unworkable, of course, we would have to stop. Meanwhile, I do understand that action will be taken to -- to see whether we can get the other system functioning as well. Mr. Russo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This would actually be a suitable time to break in my examination, if the Court wanted to allow some time for Mr. Misetic's argument and Ms. Gustafson's response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, this is new arithmetics, two times one minute, it's 12 minutes. That's -- and Ms. Gustafson has not arrived yet but she will arrive.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: She will arrive momentarily, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's be wise and perhaps not try to force matters. Mr. Konings, we'd like to see you back tomorrow, and I'd like to instruct you, that you should not speak with anyone about the testimony, either the testimony already given or the testimony still to be given in the day or days to come. We'd like to see you back tomorrow, quarter past 2.00. Madam Registrar, if I'm not mistaken, in this same courtroom, number I. Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RUSSO
utterances.text: And if I could just address very quickly, Mr. President, Mr. Kehoe raised a disclosure issue with regard to my question about the cluster munitions, and I will simply point out that this was in fact included in Lieutenant-Colonel Konings' proofing note, in fact, in the very first paragraph of the proofing note. I'm happy to provide another copy of it, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think everyone has to log on to the system again to make it work. Yes, proofing notes, of course, the Chamber is unaware of any proofing notes. If this causes still some problems, Mr. Kehoe, then, of course, the Chamber would like to be informed about it. If you are satisfied with the answer ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: At this point, Judge, we just let it go. He just said he doesn't know, but I thought we were -- the purpose of this was not to elicit evidence in the negative but to develop information about what actually happened. To the extent that it was a development of evidence in the negative, yes, it's reflected there. But I was speculating or thought we were going into something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You just let it go for the time being. Ms. Gustafson, we have invited you because Mr. Misetic would like to make a further one-minute submission on the Milutinovic case you referred to. Mr. Misetic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 14th day of January, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.
